content.title: Review of "UDA semantic segmentation via pseudo-label fusion"
content.review:
This paper proposes a pseudo label fusion framework for unsupervised domain adaptation in the context of semantic segmentation. The proposed method generates fused pseudo labels by aggregating multiple teacher model’s pseudo labels. Then, the fused pseudo labels are used to train a student model to perform semantic segmentation in the target domain. Experiments have demonstrated that the proposed method could achieve better results than SOTA. Below are some comments.

Question 1: The main contribution of this work is to combine the advantages of different UDA methods to produce more reliable pseudo-labels through ensemble learning. Although the proposed method achieves excellent performance on multiple semantic segmentation datasets, its innovation is insufficient. Regardless of model ensemble, the innovation proposed in this paper focuses only on how to fuse pseudo-labels generated by different teacher models, which seems not enough for a ICLR paper.

Question 2: This paper describes that in UDA, the methods based on adversarial learning are more time-consuming and laborious than that based on self-learning methods. However, the method proposed in this paper requires the training of multiple teacher networks, which should be more time-consuming. It lacks timing results to support this claim.

Question 3: In 3.3.2, the construction of H^fused is not clear. What does the U in H^fused=U_(k\inK)H_i^c(k) represent?

Question 4: This paper proposes that PLF can combine the advantages of different UDA models. However, according to the results in Table 3, the IOU of class "train" is 0, which is far lower than the IOU of class "train" in teacher models, such as CBST and MRKLD. What is the reason for this?

Question 5: Why are the teacher models used in GTA5 to Cityscapes different from that used in SYNTHIA to Cityscapes? Is it because of the side effects of using more teacher models in the SYNTHIA to Cityscapes scene?

Question 6: The ordinate in Figure 1 shouldn't be mIoU it should be IoU. Are the last two formulas on the penultimate line of page 5 wrong?

content.title: Response to Reviewer #4 (part 2/2)
content.comment:
- ***Performance***
As shown in Table 3, the results achieved by the proposed technique outperform all of the contemporary methods by a large margin in both of the GTA5->Cityscapes and the SYNTHIA->Cityscapes benchmarks, revealing the merits of the proposed method.  

> We provide the re-organized Table 3 in the following link: https://i.imgur.com/ct0s7Hj.png

We believe that our work pioneers this direction for semantic segmentation based UDA, thus contains a substantial research value as well as potential merits and insights for similar research areas.

We sincerely hope that the above explanations and the experimental evidence can adequately address the concerns from the reviewer.

---
***Reference***
[1] L. Breiman. Stacked regressions. Machine learning, pages
49–64, 1996.

---

Q2: This paper describes that in UDA, the methods based on adversarial learning are more time-consuming and laborious than that based on self-learning methods. However, the method proposed in this paper requires the training of multiple teacher networks, which should be more time-consuming. It lacks timing results to support this claim.

A2: We sincerely appreciate the thoughtful and constructive suggestion from the reviewer and agree with it. We have already removed this claim in the updated manuscript.

---

Q3: In 3.3.2, the construction of H^fused is not clear. What does the U in $H^{fused}=U_(k \in K)H_i^c(k)$ represent?

A3: We would like to thank the reviewer for raising this question. The symbol $∪$ in this paper denotes the union operator, and represents “the collection of the corresponding certainty values from the teacher models.”

> The union operator: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_(set_theory)

We have incorporated the definition of $∪$ in the updated manuscript, and hope that the above explanation has addressed the question from the reviewer.

---

Q4: This paper proposes that PLF can combine the advantages of different UDA models. However, according to the results in Table 3, the IOU of class "train" is 0, which is far lower than the IOU of class "train" in teacher models, such as CBST and MRKLD. What is the reason for this?

A4: We would like to thank the reviewer for raising the question, and would like to address it in terms of two aspects. First, the low IoU of this semantic class is actually caused by the data imbalance problem in the training dataset. Since the presence of the semantic class "train" is very sparse in both the source and the target domains, all of the teacher models’ predicted certainties for this class are consistently low. 

The second reason is that during the filtering stage of the proposed pseudo label fusion procedure described in Section 3.3, the filtering threshold applied is the same for all the semantic classes (i.e., 0.9 as described in Section 4.2). Therefore, the pseudo labels of the "train" class are often removed during the process as long as the predicted certainties from the teacher models are not sufficiently high, resulting in a loss of information about this semantic class. This shortcoming may potentially be mitigated by customizing different rectification thresholds for different semantic classes. However, it may induce additional efforts in searching optimal values for different filtering thresholds.  

We hope that the above explanations can address the reviewer's question.

---

Q5: Why are the teacher models used in GTA5 to Cityscapes different from that used in SYNTHIA to Cityscapes? Is it because of the side effects of using more teacher models in the SYNTHIA to Cityscapes scene?

A5: We appreciate the reviewer for asking this question, and is glad to address this concern as follows. 

The reason behind the alternation of the teacher models selected for the two benchmarks is that the experimental results of DACS are not reproducible in the SYNTHIA to Cityscapes benchmark by their officially released codes (the link to their Github repository is available below). Therefore, it is removed from the ensemble.

> The link to DACS's official Github repository for the reviewer's reference: https://github.com/vikolss/DACS

We hope the above explanations can address the reviewer's concern.

---

Q6: The ordinate in Figure 1 shouldn't be mIoU it should be IoU. Are the last two formulas on the penultimate line of page 5 wrong?

A6: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer for pointing out our typos, and have already corrected them in the updated manuscript (***which has been uploaded to the ICLR website***).

content.title: Response to Reviewer #4 (part 1/2)
content.comment:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for spending time and providing valuable feedback. We would like to address the concerns from the reviewer by providing our responses as well as our additional experimental results.

---

Q1: The main contribution of this work is to combine the advantages of different UDA methods to produce more reliable pseudo-labels through ensemble learning. Although the proposed method achieves excellent performance on multiple semantic segmentation datasets, its innovation is insufficient. Regardless of model ensemble, ***the innovation proposed in this paper focuses only on how to fuse pseudo-labels generated by different teacher models***, which seems not enough for a ICLR paper.

A1: 
We would like to thank the reviewer for raising this question, and would be glad to address the concerns from the reviewer.  

We would first like to bring to the reviewer's kind attention that ***the contributions of this work are not limited to the fusion methods***. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to integrate ensemble learning, output-level knowledge distillation, and pseudo label fusion into the application domain of semantic segmentation based UDA. Finding the right and new place for these techniques is one of the core themes of research.  In addition, ***the selection of the right fusion method plays an essential role in the success of semantic segmentation based UDA***. The innovations of this research are summarized as follows. 

- ***Usage of ensemble learning***
Unlike previous works that utilize ensemble learning to produce representations through amortizing the predictions of different teacher models, our work employs ensemble learning to utilize different distributions of semantic class labels in the ensemble. As shown in the figure below:

>The figure that demonstrates the variation of the distributions of semantic class labels among different models is available at the link:https://i.imgur.com/wlU60F9.png

- ***Investigation and analysis of the fusion functions***
Due to the variation of the training methods, the per-class performance of the contemporary semantic segmentation based UDA methods has a tendency to vary by a considerable margin. In our work, three channel-wise fusion functions (i.e., certainty fusion, priority fusion, and majority fusion) are thoroughly investigated, compared, and analyzed to serve as the aggregation function of the ensemble for preserving the integrity of the predictions from different semantic class channels and handling consensus pixels as well as disagreements. These fusion functions adopt a different fusion scheme compared to the traditional fusion function, i.e., bagging [1], in that ***our pseudo labels are fused on the basis of channels instead of pixels***. Furthermore, the experimental results reveal that the proposed fusion method is able to generate high-quality pseudo labels. As shown in the table below, our framework with majority fusion achieves 91.38% of the oracle performance, indicating that ***the fused pseudo labels produced by our method are highly resemble to the ground truth annotations***.

> The comparison to [1] is provided in the following link for the reviewer's reference: https://i.imgur.com/bFKfIAa.png

> The table for comparing the resemblance of our pseudo labels to the ground truth is provided in the following link for the reviewer's reference: https://i.imgur.com/287RerZ.png 

- ***Evolution with Time***
We would also like to respectfully point out that the proposed PLF method possess the capability to evolve with time.  We have incorporated an additional set of experimental results into the updated manuscript to demonstrate these advantages. The experimental results on ***PLF-3M*** and ***PLF-3D*** reveal that when more teacher models trained with different methods are included in the ensemble, the higher the performance of our framework achieves. This observation suggests that the inclusion of more teacher models in the ensemble is beneficial to our framework’s performance. The insight is that different training methods may lead to different decision boundaries among the teacher models, which can be potentially utilized by the ensemble learning framework to improve the performance. We would also like to bring to the kind attention of the reviewer that the teacher models in the below table are organized in chronological order. This validates that our design possesses the potential to evolve with time, since a newly proposed UDA training method can be added into the ensemble and further increases the performance of our framework.

> The additional experimental results are also provided in the following link for reviewer's reference: https://i.imgur.com/Fe13WA4.png

The claims and the method are correct. The motivation of this paper is the performance can be further enhanced by incorporating knowledge from multiple models. However, the proposed framework is very similar to the multi-teacher distillation, such as [*],[#]. Meanwhile, the certainty fusion and priority fusion methods are widely used in self-training. So the novelty is limited.

The authors have extensive experiments in Table 1, which reports the number of trainable parameters, the inference speed, and the semantic segmentation performance of the PLF framework with different student network backbones. The PLF achieves good performance even with compact and fast backbones compared with the state-of-art methods. In Table 2, a baseline ensemble is needed. Since the PLF use DACS, R-MRNet, CBST, and MRKLD models as teachers, the traditional ensembles which obtained through averaging the final predictions across all teacher models should be compared with the proposed method.

The paper organization could be improved, especially in section 5.

content.title: Response to Reviewer #2 (part 1/2)
content.comment:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for spending time and providing valuable feedback. We would like to address the concerns from the reviewer by providing our responses as follows.

---

Q1: However, the proposed framework is very similar to the multi-teacher distillation, such as ***MEAL: Multi-Model Ensemble via Adversarial Learning***, and ***Multiple Expert Brainstorming for Domain Adaptive Person Re-identification***. Meanwhile, ***the certainty fusion and priority fusion methods are widely used in self-training***. So the novelty is limited.


A1:

***We are afraid that there might be some misunderstanding***.

We would like to bring to the reviewer's kind attention that our work is different from the two papers ***in terms of motivation, methodology, and applied domain***.  In addition, ***certainty fusion and priority fusion are only used as the baselines to be compared with the majority fusion method*** (as described in Section 3), which is discussed in the analysis in Section 5.1 to validate why ***the majority fusion method is the one selected throughout our experiments***.  

In the following paragraphs, we would like to discuss in depth where the two papers differ from ours. First of all, these two papers do not belong to the field of semantic segmentation based UDA, as ***the first one aims to deal with supervised image classification problems*** while ***the other focuses on person re-identification  UDA tasks***. Our proposed methods and all of the baseline approaches compared in Table 3 and analyzed in Section 2, nevertheless, are fully dedicated to the semantic segmentation based UDA domain.

Second, from the perspective of motivation, these two works adopt ensemble learning because of its potential performance benefits, and employ knowledge distillation techniques to keep the computational costs at a manageable level. In contrast, ***the motivation of our framework is to investigate a method to integrate the knowledge learned by developed UDA models***. Our observation (Fig. 1) shows that due to the variation of the training methods, the per-class performance of the contemporary semantic segmentation based UDA methods have a tendency to vary by a considerable margin, which can be potentially utilized by the ensemble learning framework [1]. In order to preserve the integrity of the predictions from different semantic class channels, ***three channel-wise pseudo label fusion functions are thoroughly investigated, compared, and analyzed in this paper.***

Third, in terms of methodology, the student model in [2] is trained to learn the embedding of one of the randomly picked teacher model in the ensemble. Therefore, the concept of fusion function is not present in their framework. On the other hand, the approach in [3] adopted an average function to aggregate the predictions of the ensemble, and aims to produce a representation through amortizing the predictions of different teacher models.  In our work, three channel-wise fusion functions are presented in Section 3 to serve as the aggregation function of the ensemble for handling consensus pixels as well as disagreements.  Among these three methods, majority fusion is analyzed in Section 5.1 and shown to be the most effective one, while certainty fusion and priority fusion only serve as baselines for comparison purposes.  As a consequence, ***the experimental results presented in Table 3 are all based on the majority fusion method***.

In conclusion, although these two works share some similarities with ours in terms of the technique used, they should not be confused with our work since ***the application domains, the motivations, as well as the methodologies***. We still appreciate the suggestions from the reviewer and ***have included them as our citations in the updated manuscript***. 

We hope that the above explanations have adequately addressed the cocncerns from the reviewer.

---
***Reference***
- [1] D. Opitz and R. Maclin. Popular ensemble methods: An
empirical study. Journal of artificial intelligence research, 1999.
- [2] Z. Shen, Z. He, and X. Xue. Meal: Multi-model ensemble via
adversarial learning. In Proc. of the AAAI Conf. on Artificial
Intelligence, 2019.
- [3] Y. Zhai, Q. Ye, S. Lu, M. Jia, R. Ji, and Y. Tian. Multiple
expert brainstorming for domain adaptive person reidentification.
arXiv:2007.01546, 2020.

content.title: Insufficient comparison with competing methods, unclear motivation, and incremental technical contribution.
content.review:
The paper proposes a method for cross-domain semantic segmentation with pseudo-label fusion and aims to better capture the label distribution in the target domain. The proposed framework consists of training an ensemble of teacher networks, fusing the predictions of the teacher models and distilling the knowledge in the fused prediction with a student network. Through distillation, the student network is able to approximate the ground-truth label distribution for target images. Following the framework, the authors proposed different approaches for pseudo label fusion, namely certainty, priority and majority fusion and explored the effect of each on different backbones on UDA between several dataset pairs. 

The paper is well-organised and the method is well-explained, I am also happy to see that the method works for several different architectures including deeplab v3+, and DRN 50. However I have several concerns regarding the paper:
(1) Cross-domain semantic segmentation is a quite active research field. However, I found the recent work in this space (such as [A][B]) is not discussed/compared in experiments. Therefore it's not fully clear where the method stands compared to the SOTA.
(2) The technical contribution also seems incremental, the main contribution lies in the approaches to fuse teacher models, which may have limited impact on the work for UDA. 
(3) The motivation is also not fully clear to me, it is somewhat expected that ensemble of different predictions can improve the performance. However, whether this is a key problem in cross-domain semantic segmentation is a bit arguable.
(4) In Table 3, the proposed method achieves a clear improvement between Deeplab v3+ and v2 in Synthia to CS (51.76 vs 48.45), however the gap is much smaller in GTAV to CS (57.65 vs 57.15). I am curious what's the reason behind this?
(5) The presentation can be improved, currently the tables are not easy to read. 

[A] FDA: Fourier Domain Adaptation for Semantic Segmentation
[B] Cross-Domain Semantic Segmentation via Domain-Invariant Interactive Relation Transfer

--
Some of my concerns are addressed in the response, I appreciate the provided comparisons and results. However, I am still not fully convinced that the technical contribution is sufficient. To reflect this, I slightly bumped up the rating to 5.

content.title: Pseudo-label fusion and distillation for semantic segmentation domain adaptation
content.review:
**Summary**:
This paper introduces a new pipeline, called pseudo label fusion (PLF) to deal with the semantic segmentation domain adaptation. The main novelty is that it leverages multiple networks to improve the predictions’ robustness. Three different aggregation functions are designed to combine the results from different teacher networks. A student network is also used to distill out the information from the teacher model. Authors conduct experiments on the standard settings to verify the effectiveness of the proposed pipeline.

**Pros**:
+ The whole idea makes sense. A new framework is proposed for semantic segmentation domain adaptation. Several variants of aggregation functions are also designed.
+ Authors conduct comprehensive experiments to show the effectiveness of the proposed pipeline. Parameters analysis is also performed for the design choice.
+ Overall, the paper is well written and well organized.

**Concerns**: 
- For figure 1, I wonder why the mIOU is very low for train class if using PLF? What is the potential reason behind it?
- One concern is about novelty. If I understand the whole context correctly, the teacher-student distillation framework has been explored to reduce the model size and computational cost. Using multiple networks to do ensembles is also touched by the previous works. This paper applies these techniques to the application of domain adaptation. I feel the whole pipeline is not novel enough to reach the standard of this venue.
- For the multiple teacher networks, do they use different backbones? If that, is it possible to have the experiments to show the results using the same architecture, but with different initializations or training procedures? I am curious about the performance of this experiment.
- As we have multiple teacher networks, is it possible to have the ablation study to show how number of teacher network affects the final performance?

**Minor Comments**:
* the last line on page 5. There are repeated definitions of $R^{fused}$.

Overall, I prefer the rating as below the threshold at the current stage. The main reason is the limited novelty. Hope the authors could address my concerns or questions in the rebuttal period.

The second reason is that during the filtering stage of the proposed pseudo label fusion procedure described in Section 3.3, the filtering threshold applied is the same for all the semantic classes (i.e., 0.9 as described in Section 4.2). Therefore, the pseudo labels of the "train" class are often removed during the process as long as the predicted certainties from the teacher models are not sufficiently high, resulting in a loss of information about this semantic class. This shortcoming may potentially be mitigated by customizing different rectification thresholds for different semantic classes. However, it may induce additional efforts in searching optimal values for different filtering thresholds.  

We hope that the above explanations can address the reviewer's question.

---

Q2: One concern is about novelty. If I understand the whole context correctly, the teacher-student distillation framework has been explored to reduce the model size and computational cost. Using multiple networks to do ensembles is also touched by previous works. This paper applies these techniques to the application of domain adaptation. I feel the whole pipeline is not novel enough to reach the standard of this venue.

A2: 
As pointed out by the reviewer, ensemble learning was used for the purpose of distillation and reduction of the computational costs, but has not yet been applied to the domain of semantic segmentation based UDA. We are afraid that there might be some misunderstanding from the reviewer that, the core theme of this paper is not the teacher-student framework itself. However, every technique has its own niche, and finding the right and new place for an existing technique is the spirit of research. Although the concept of the ensemble framework has been used in other areas, its original purpose was not for enhancing the performance of UDA. This work casts the concept of ensemble learning to the domain of semantic segmentation based UDA, as the proposed PLF framework employs ensemble models to enhance the quality of the fused pseudo labels. Moreover, the Majory Fusion technique applied to the predictions of the ensemble has  never been attempted or discussed by the literature before. Furthermore, we would like to bring to the reviewer's kind attention that the results achieved by the proposed technique outperform all of the contemporary methods by a large margin, revealing the merits of the proposed method.

As a result, the main contribution of this paper is the investigation of the pseudo label fusion techniques for improving the performance of semantic segmentation based UDA.  Although a teacher-student based framework is adopted, we believe that our work pioneers this direction for semantic segmentation based UDA, thus contains a substantial research value as well as potential merits and insights for similar research areas.

We hope that the above explanations have adequately addressed the reviewer's concerns.
